name: Acromioclavicular (AC) Joint Injury
summary: Injury to the AC and, in higher grades, coracoclavicular ligaments, commonly after a fall onto the shoulder.

looksLike: Pain with cross-body movement or pushing
Visible step deformity in higher-grade injury
firstSteps: Protect from painful compression and heavy lifting
Use sling briefly only if needed for comfort and clinician-directed
Maintain elbow, wrist and hand movement; begin shoulder ROM as tolerated

tests.name: Cross-Body Adduction Test
tests.purpose: Reproduce AC-region symptoms with horizontal adduction; test is not diagnostic alone.
tests.positive: Familiar focal pain at AC joint.

stages.label: Protection, Education & Symptom-Guided Loading
stages.goal: Address safety, settle excessive irritability and maintain useful movement.
do: Protect from painful compression and heavy lifting
Use sling briefly only if needed for comfort and clinician-directed
Maintain elbow, wrist and hand movement; begin shoulder ROM as tolerated
moveOn: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Capacity
stages.goal: Restore the specific strength, mobility and control required by the condition.
when: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.
do: Strengthen rotator cuff and scapular muscles
Reintroduce pushing, carrying and cross-body tasks
dose: Band external rotation and rows: 2–3 x 10–15
moveOn: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.

stages.label: Functional Restoration & Return to Activity
stages.goal: Rebuild real-world, occupational or sporting capacity.
when: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.
do: Restore push-up, lifting and work-specific capacity
Consider orthopaedic review for persistent symptoms or high-grade injury
dose: Sport-specific contact exposure only after adequate healing and clearance
moveOn: Full task exposure is completed progressively.
No clinically meaningful deterioration during the following 24 hours.

returnCriteria: Painless or acceptable cross-body and overhead tasks
Strength and contact tolerance appropriate to injury grade

structures: Coracoclavicular conoid and trapezoid ligaments in higher-grade injuries
mechanism: Fall onto outstretched arm less commonly
classification: Rockwood I–VI; grading requires clinical and imaging context
investigations: Radiographs when fracture, significant separation or higher-grade injury suspected.
Urgent medical assessment for deformity, skin compromise or neurovascular findings.
manual: Gentle shoulder and scapular mobility may help secondary stiffness.
Avoid direct forceful AC joint mobilisation in acute injury.
modalities: Ice may be used briefly for comfort.
Sling is short-term comfort support, not prolonged immobilisation.
mistakes: Repeatedly stressing the AC joint early
Using deformity alone to determine function
pearls: Rockwood grade and functional symptoms both inform management.
Many low-grade injuries recover with progressive non-operative care.

tests.name: Cross-Body Adduction Test
tests.purpose: Reproduce AC-region symptoms with horizontal adduction; test is not diagnostic alone.
tests.positive: Familiar focal pain at AC joint.
tests.patientPosition: Seated or standing; passively bring arm across chest while stabilising trunk.
tests.therapistPosition: Position yourself to observe and stabilise the relevant segment without forcing the movement.
tests.handPlacement: Use comfortable, controlled contact appropriate to the test; avoid painful compression or excessive force.
procedure: Explain the test and obtain consent.
Screen contraindications and compare sides when appropriate.
Perform the movement slowly and apply only the required resistance or stress.
Record familiar symptom reproduction, range, strength and side-to-side difference.
tests.interpretation: Supports AC involvement when history and local tenderness agree; consider imaging after trauma.
tests.clinicalNote: A special test modifies clinical probability; it does not confirm a diagnosis in isolation.
